data.title: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pseudoxanthoma elasticum** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. What is pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE)?**
- Autosomal recessive multisystem disorder of ectopic mineralisation (calcification) and fragmentation of elastic fibres in skin, eyes (Bruch's membrane) and arteries — ABCC6 mutations (liver transporter; low plasma pyrophosphate — calcification inhibitor); ENPP1/GGCX in PXE-like disorders

**Q2. Cutaneous features.**
- Onset in childhood/adolescence: small yellowish papules coalescing into cobblestoned 'plucked chicken skin' / 'Moroccan leather' plaques on the sides of the neck (first site), axillae, antecubital and popliteal fossae, groin, periumbilical (flexural areas); later lax redundant folds; oral mucosa (lower lip) yellow papules; perforating PXE (periumbilical, multiparous women)

**Q3. Systemic features.**
- Eyes: angioid streaks (breaks in calcified Bruch's membrane — grey-brown lines radiating from optic disc), 'peau d'orange' fundus, choroidal neovascularisation → haemorrhage → central vision loss
- Cardiovascular: premature atherosclerosis, intermittent claudication (peripheral arterial disease), reduced pulses, hypertension, angina, MI, stroke; GI haemorrhage (gastric arteries), mitral valve prolapse

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Fragmented, clumped, curled and calcified elastic fibres in the mid and deep reticular dermis — highlighted by Verhoeff–van Gieson (elastic) and von Kossa (calcium) stains; perforation of elastic fibres in perforating PXE

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- PXE-like papillary dermal elastolysis, solar elastosis, cutis laxa, late-onset focal dermal elastosis, perforating calcific elastosis, D-penicillamine-induced elastosis, amyloidosis, xanthomas, lax skin syndromes, Buschke–Ollendorff syndrome, white fibrous papulosis of neck

**Q6. Diagnostic criteria (Plomp 2010).**
- Major: characteristic skin lesions with histology (fragmented calcified elastic fibres); angioid streaks/peau d'orange (retina); two pathogenic ABCC6 mutations
- Minor: one ABCC6 mutation, PXE in a first-degree relative

**Q7. Management.**
- No cure; multidisciplinary follow-up: annual eye examination (Amsler grid self-monitoring; intravitreal anti-VEGF — bevacizumab, ranibizumab, aflibercept for choroidal neovascularisation), cardiovascular risk control (no smoking, lipid/BP control, exercise), avoid contact sports (eye trauma), caution with aspirin/anticoagulants (GI bleeding)
- Dietary calcium in normal amounts; magnesium supplementation and etidronate (bisphosphonate — reduced arterial calcification in trial) under study
- Cosmetic: excision of lax skin folds (plastic surgery), fillers; genetic counselling

**Q8. Describe skin findings in detail.**
- Small yellowish papules coalescing into 'plucked chicken skin' or cobblestone plaques on flexural sites — sides of neck (first), axillae, antecubital and popliteal fossae, groin, periumbilical; later lax redundant skin folds; oral mucosa (inner lip) yellow papules; 'perforating' PXE with calcified elastic extrusion

**Q9. Systemic features in detail.**
- Cardiovascular: premature atherosclerosis, intermittent claudication, angina, hypertension (renovascular), mitral valve prolapse, GI haemorrhage (gastric — submucosal vessel calcification), cerebrovascular events; ocular: angioid streaks, choroidal neovascularisation (central vision loss)

**Q10. What is periumbilical perforating PXE?**
- Acquired localised PXE in multiparous obese black women — hyperpigmented plaques with keratotic papules around umbilicus; elastic fibre calcification with transepidermal elimination; no systemic disease

**Q11. Acquired PXE-like changes — causes.**
- Penicillamine (elastosis perforans serpiginosa and PXE-like), saltpetre exposure, calcium salts, chronic kidney disease (calcific elastosis), β-thalassaemia/ sickle cell (PXE-like phenotype with angioid streaks)

**Q12. Management in detail.**
- No cure; multidisciplinary — ophthalmology (Amsler grid self-monitoring, anti-VEGF intravitreal for neovascularisation), cardiovascular risk control (statins, BP, stop smoking, exercise), avoid NSAIDs/ anticoagulants where possible (GI bleeding), avoid contact sports; cosmetic surgery for redundant skin; trials of oral pyrophosphate, etidronate (slows arterial calcification)

**Q13. Define and classify genodermatoses (PYQ).**
- Inherited disorders with skin manifestations — by inheritance: AD (NF1, TSC, Darier, Hailey–Hailey, EBS), AR (XP, lamellar ichthyosis, PXE, oculocutaneous albinism), X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis, Fabry, Wiskott–Aldrich), X-linked dominant (IP, Goltz, CHILD, Conradi), mitochondrial, mosaic (epidermal naevi, McCune–Albright, Proteus)
- By function: keratinisation (ichthyoses, PPK), adhesion (EB), pigmentation (albinism, piebaldism), DNA repair (XP, Bloom), connective tissue (EDS, PXE, cutis laxa), tumour syndromes (NF, TSC, Gorlin), vascular (HHT), ectodermal dysplasias, immunodeficiency

**Q14. Explain the molecular basis.**
- Autosomal recessive ABCC6 mutations (liver transporter) → low plasma inorganic pyrophosphate (anti-mineralisation factor) → ectopic calcification of elastic fibres in skin, retina (Bruch's membrane), arteries; PXE-like phenotype with GGCX mutations (with clotting factor deficiency) and ENPP1 (GACI)

**Q15. Describe ocular findings.**
- Angioid streaks (breaks in calcified Bruch's membrane radiating from optic disc), peau d'orange of retina, comet tails; complications — choroidal neovascularisation → haemorrhage and loss of central vision; treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections; avoid contact sports/ head trauma

**Q16. What special stains are used?**
- Von Kossa (calcium — black), Verhoeff–van Gieson (fragmented, curled, clumped elastic fibres in mid/deep dermis), Alizarin red; elastic fibres look 'raveled wool'

## Quick spotter facts
- Plucked-chicken yellow papules on sides of neck + angioid streaks — PXE (ABCC6)
- Calcified fragmented elastic fibres (von Kossa)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Disorders of elastic tissue). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
